title: Council Condemns Paul of Samosata — Early Heresy Prosecution
description: The Council of Antioch (264 CE, with follow-up in 268 CE) condemned Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch, for the heresy of dynamic monarchianism — the view that Christ was a man adopted by God rather than eternally divine. This constituted one of the early formal heresy prosecutions establishing patterns of ecclesiastical investigation, accusation, and condemnation that would be elaborated into the inquisitorial process. The case also involved allegations of personal misconduct and financial irregularities alongside theological error, prefiguring the typical pattern of heresy charges bundled with other accusations. Paul's case required the unusual intervention of the Roman Emperor Aurelian to enforce the council's judgment.
historiographical_note: Henry Chadwick and Rowan Williams have analyzed the Paul of Samosata case as a formative moment in the development of ecclesiastical heresy-investigation procedures, establishing patterns later institutionalized in the medieval Inquisition.
source_method: Published scholarship; Eusebius Ecclesiastical History 7.27-30; secondary patristic scholarship
